topic.subject: social
topic.title: The Harappan civilisation
topic.scope: planned cities, citadel, drains, Great Bath, Lothal dockyard, Dholavira, seals and script, end of the cities

nodes.name: Economic and Social Life
external_prereqs: difference between raw materials and finished goods

misconceptions.statement: The Citadel was a military fort used for fighting wars.
misconceptions.why: Students associate high walls and raised platforms with modern or medieval forts.
misconceptions.fix: The Citadel was a raised area likely used for special public buildings or by the ruling class, not necessarily for warfare.

probe.question: Why was the western part of Harappan cities built on a high platform?
probe.wrong_answer: To place cannons and soldiers to attack enemies.

misconceptions.root_belief: ancient structures always served military purposes

misconceptions.statement: Harappan houses were weak because they were made of mud.
misconceptions.why: Students assume ancient people did not have the technology to bake bricks.
misconceptions.fix: Harappans used interlocking patterns of baked bricks that were so strong they lasted for thousands of years.

probe.question: What made Harappan walls last for 4000 years?
probe.wrong_answer: They were made of simple dried mud.

misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE studies on student ideas of materials

misconceptions.statement: Ancient people didn't care about hygiene because they lived long ago.
misconceptions.why: A general bias that progress in health is only a modern phenomenon.
misconceptions.fix: Harappan cities had a very advanced drainage system with covered drains and inspection holes for cleaning.

probe.question: How did Harappans handle waste water from their houses?
probe.wrong_answer: They threw it on the streets because they lacked toilets.

misconceptions.root_belief: past people were less hygienic than us

misconceptions.statement: The Great Bath was a public swimming pool for recreation.
misconceptions.why: Students map the structure to modern leisure facilities like club pools.
misconceptions.fix: The Great Bath was likely used for special ritual bathing or religious ceremonies.

probe.question: What was the most likely use of the Great Bath in Mohenjodaro?
probe.wrong_answer: It was a place for children to learn swimming.

misconceptions.root_belief: modern functions apply to ancient forms

misconceptions.statement: Harappans used iron to make their strong tools and weapons.
misconceptions.why: Iron is the most common metal students associate with 'strong' tools.
misconceptions.fix: Harappans lived in the Bronze Age; they used copper and bronze, but iron was unknown to them.

probe.question: Which metal was NOT used by the Harappan craftsmen?

misconceptions.root_belief: iron has always been the primary metal
misconceptions.source_hint: Common historical chronology errors in middle school

misconceptions.statement: Harappan seals were used as coins to buy things in the market.
misconceptions.why: Students see small flat objects with symbols and think of modern currency.
misconceptions.fix: Seals were used to stamp bags of goods to ensure they weren't tampered with during trade.

probe.question: What was the main purpose of a Harappan seal?
probe.wrong_answer: To pay for bread or clothes like a coin.

misconceptions.root_belief: small stamped objects are always money

misconceptions.statement: We have read many books written by Harappan kings.
misconceptions.why: Students assume that because they had a script, we must be able to read it.
misconceptions.fix: Although they had a script, it has not been deciphered yet, so we cannot read what they wrote.

probe.question: What do we know about the stories written in the Harappan script?
probe.wrong_answer: We know all their history because we read their books.

misconceptions.root_belief: all ancient writing is understood today

misconceptions.statement: The entire civilization was destroyed by a single big war.
misconceptions.why: Dramatic single-event explanations are easier to remember than complex environmental ones.
misconceptions.fix: There was no single cause; factors like rivers drying up, deforestation, and flooding likely led to the decline.

probe.question: What caused the end of the Harappan cities?
probe.wrong_answer: A giant battle where everyone was killed at once.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on causal reasoning

misconceptions.statement: All Harappan cities were exactly the same and had only two parts.
misconceptions.why: Overgeneralizing the Mohenjodaro/Harappa model to all sites.
misconceptions.fix: While many had two parts, Dholavira was unique because it was divided into three distinct parts.

probe.question: How was Dholavira different from other Harappan cities?
probe.wrong_answer: It was exactly the same as Mohenjodaro.

misconceptions.root_belief: all members of a category are identical

misconceptions.statement: The dockyard at Lothal was for small fishing boats only.
misconceptions.why: Underestimating the scale of ancient international trade.
misconceptions.fix: The dockyard was a huge tank where ships from distant lands like Mesopotamia came to trade.

probe.question: What kind of travel happened at the Lothal dockyard?
probe.wrong_answer: Only local people catching fish in the river.

misconceptions.statement: Harappans only used stones they found on the ground for beads.
misconceptions.why: Lack of understanding of 'raw material' procurement and processing.
misconceptions.fix: They traveled long distances to get specific stones like carnelian and used specialized drills to make beads.

probe.question: Where did Harappans get the materials for their beautiful beads?
probe.wrong_answer: They just picked up random pebbles from the street.

misconceptions.root_belief: ancient people didn't plan for resources

misconceptions.statement: When the cities ended, all the Harappan people died out.
misconceptions.why: Confusing the abandonment of urban centers with the extinction of a population.
misconceptions.fix: The cities were abandoned, but people likely moved to new settlements in the east and south.

probe.question: What happened to the people when the Harappan cities declined?
probe.wrong_answer: Every single person died because of a plague.

misconceptions.root_belief: end of city means end of race
misconceptions.source_hint: AAAS Project 2061 - ideas about extinction vs migration

problems: misconception dropped: 'Harappans only used stones they found on the groun'
